Before we start

How this class works

Ask anything

If a question blocks you, ask right away. Otherwise park it for the Q&A at the end.

Focus on the message

Don't worry about every term. Slides and templates will be in your LMS after class.

Be honest

Share real examples and real feedback. The anonymous class survey helps us improve.

Practise live

We'll rewrite updates, map stakeholders and run a mock interview together.

Bring your work

Use a product you know (your job or your favourite app) for every exercise.

Have fun

Good communicators are curious and generous. Let's practise both.

01
Part 1

Communication is the job

Why the best PMs win on clarity, not on process.

SkillNavora · Week 6
Foundations

Why communication is the PM's core tool

PMs rarely have formal authority over the people who build, sell or support the product. Influence comes from clarity, evidence, trust and consistency.

Most PM failures are communication failures: an unclear problem, an unshared trade-off, a surprise, or a decision nobody wrote down.
  • Start with the answer, then support it
  • Know your audience: what decision do they need to make?
  • Make trade-offs explicit: options, cost, benefit, risk
  • Label facts, assumptions and opinions
  • Write it down: decisions, owners, dates
  • No surprises: share bad news early, with a plan
  • Listen more than you talk
SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM
Mindset

Two habits of great communicators

Habit 1

Extreme ownership

If the team misunderstood, the message wasn't clear enough. Own the outcome of every update: did the right people understand and act? Follow up until they do.

Ask after every important message: "Who needed to act, and did they?"

Habit 2

Audience empathy

Start from what the listener cares about, the words they use and the decision they face. An engineer, a CFO and a support lead need different versions of the same news.

Rewrite the first line for each audience before you send.

Content over process. Rituals, trackers and templates matter less than the substance: the problem, the evidence, the decision and the trade-off. Fix the content first; the process is a vehicle.
SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM
A system

Communication is a product system

Design every update the way you design a feature: for a user, with a goal, through the right channel, with a way to learn if it worked.

AudienceWho needs to act?
MessageWhat must be clear?
ChannelWhere will it travel?
FeedbackHow will you learn?

02
Part 2

A framework for every message

Audience × objective × approach.

SkillNavora · Week 6
Framework

Audience, objective, approach

1 · Audience

  • Core team (eng, design, data)
  • Dependency teams
  • Your manager and leadership
  • Outer circle: ops, legal, support, marketing, sales
  • Users and customers

2 · Objective

  • Educate: share context
  • Learn: get input or data
  • Influence: change a view
  • Decide: get a decision

3 · Approach

  • Content: what to say, in what order
  • Channel: doc, meeting, chat, demo
  • Cadence: one-off, weekly, per release
Before any update, write one line: "I want [audience] to [objective], so I'll [approach]." Example: "I want the Head of Payments to decide on the fee test, so I'll send a one-page brief 48 hours before Thursday's review."
SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM
Channels

Pick the channel by purpose and urgency

ChannelBest forAvoid for
Document (PRD, memo, wiki)Complex reasoning, decisions, a recordQuick questions
MeetingDebate, alignment, sensitive topicsStatus that could be written
Chat (Slack, Teams)Quick questions, coordinationDecisions, long debates, bad news
Async video (Loom)Demos, walkthroughs across time zonesAnything that needs discussion
DashboardMetrics people check themselvesExplaining why something changed
Email / newsletterWide updates, external partnersFast back-and-forth
A useful rule: decisions in documents, discussion in meetings, coordination in chat. Then link the chat thread to the doc.

Direction 1

Best practices with your core team

Involve them early

Share the why before the what. Engineers and designers often see the simplest solution.

Define responsibilities

Who owns what (RACI) prevents confusion and finger-pointing later.

Speak one language

Shared terms, a shared board and one source of truth for decisions.

Set shared goals

Agree the outcome metric together so everyone pulls the same way.

Protect focus

Batch questions, keep scope stable mid-sprint, and say no on their behalf.

Celebrate and credit

Share wins with names in public updates. Own misses yourself.

SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM

Who

  • Your manager and skip-level
  • Executives and business leaders
  • Managers of partner teams

What they want

  • Progress against goals, in numbers
  • Risks early, with your plan
  • Decisions they need to make, and by when
  • Your judgement: recommendations, not lists
1:1 notes doc · [You] / [Manager]

Direction 2

The critical-issue update

🔴 Issue update · Payment failures · Update #2 · 14:00 IST
StatusOngoing · Severity 1
Impact~8% of payments failing since 11:20; ~1,900 users affected
CauseGateway timeout after config change (confirmed)
ActionsRolled back config at 13:40; failures dropping; retry banner live
Next stepsMonitor 2h; post-mortem Thursday
Next update16:00 IST, or sooner if anything changes
OwnerPM: Asha · Eng: Rohit
  • Send the first update fast, even if incomplete
  • Same structure every time, so readers can scan
  • Facts, then actions, then the next update time
  • One owner; a single thread or channel
  • Close it out: final update plus post-mortem link
Hypothetical example.
SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM
Direction 3

The outer circle

Best practices with non-technical partners

  • Set context early, with a short pre-read
  • Repeat your goal, roadmap and progress, again and again
  • Speak their language: impact on their team, not tech details
  • Know their why, and share yours
  • Be transparent about risks and dates
  • Listen more than you talk
SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM
Direction 3

A conversation with operations

PM: We're launching 15-minute grocery delivery in Pune next month. I'd like your view on what would make it work for your team.

Head of Ops: Honestly, our dark stores can't handle evening peaks yet.

PM: That's exactly what I need to know. If we launch in two pin codes first, with orders capped at 6–9 pm, could the stores keep up?

Head of Ops: Two pin codes, yes. I'd need 6 more pickers and a week of training.

PM: Let's put that in the launch plan. I'll share the forecast by Friday so you can hire, and we'll review peak-hour data together every week.

  • Start from their constraint, not your plan
  • Offer a smaller, safer first step
  • Turn their needs into launch requirements
  • Agree a shared review rhythm
Illustrative, fictional scenario.
SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM

05
Part 5

Answer first

Structures that make your point land in seconds.

SkillNavora · Week 6
Structure

The Pyramid Principle: answer first

Recommendation: show the delivery fee in the cart this quarter
Biggest checkout leak30% leave at payment6 of 8 users cite fee surprise
Cheap and low-risk~2 person-monthsBehind a feature flag
We can prove itA/B test, 14 daysGuardrail: complaints ≤ 1.3%

Lead with the governing thought, group reasons (MECE: no overlaps, no gaps), support each with evidence. A leader can stop at any level and still have the point. Example is hypothetical.

SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM
Structure

SCQA: how to open any update, memo or pitch

SituationShared, uncontroversial context
ComplicationWhat changed or what's wrong
QuestionThe question this raises
AnswerYour recommendation, then the pyramid
Example. S: Checkout completion is 70% and our biggest growth lever this quarter. C: 30% leave at payment, and users say the fee surprises them. Q: What should we change first? A: Show the full fee in the cart, tested as a two-week A/B experiment.
SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM
Writing

BLUF and writing for busy readers

BLUF: bottom line up front

Put the conclusion or the ask in the first line, so a reader who stops there still knows what to do.

Subject: Decision needed by Thu: approve 2-week fee test
BLUF: I recommend we test early fee display for 2 weeks. I need your approval by Thursday.

Writing checklist

  • One idea per paragraph; short sentences
  • Headings and bullets readers can scan
  • Numbers with context (baseline, target, sample)
  • Plain words; define any acronym once
  • A clear ask with owner and date
  • Your vision in one elevator-pitch line at the top of specs and decks
SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM
Writing

The executive summary: one screen, top of every doc

  • The ask: the decision and the date
  • The recommendation
  • Why: 2–3 bullets with numbers
  • Risks and how you'll handle them
  • What you need: people, money, decision
  • What you're not doing
Decision needed by 15 May: approve 2 engineers for 6 weeks to test early fee display.
Recommendation: A/B test; ship only if completion rises ≥ 2 points with no rise in complaints.
Why: payment step loses 30% of starters; 6/8 users cite fee surprise; est. +2,160 orders/month (range 720–4,320).
Risks: estimate inaccuracy → label as estimate, fallback text.
Not doing: loyalty redesign until Q3.
SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM
Writing

Narrative memos and PR/FAQs

Narrative memo

Think in full sentences

Some companies (Amazon popularised it) replace slides with a written memo read silently at the start of the meeting. Prose forces complete reasoning: claims, evidence and trade-offs can't hide behind bullets.

PR/FAQ

Write the launch first

Before building, write a one-page press release from the customer's point of view, then the FAQs customers and leaders would ask. If the press release isn't exciting, rethink the idea.

SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM

Pick the structure by audience and purpose

SituationStructureShapeLength

Opinion in a meeting or stand-upPREPPoint → Reason → Example → Point30–60 s
Feedback to a colleagueSBISituation → Behaviour → Impact → ask2 min

Part 6

Storytelling

STAR, data and the stories people remember.

SkillNavora · Week 6
Storytelling

STAR turns activity into a story

Without STAR"We shipped a feature and users liked it."
With STAR"Week-2 retention had fallen to 31% (S). I had to bring it back without new engineering headcount (T). We interviewed 12 churned users, simplified onboarding from 5 steps to 3 and added a progress nudge (A). Retention rose to 36% in six weeks, measured in an A/B test (R)."
  • Situation: context and the stakes, with a number
  • Task: what you had to achieve, and the constraint
  • Action: what you did (say "I", not only "we")
  • Result: the measured outcome, or say it wasn't measured
  • Add a one-line learning
Use STAR in demos, leadership reviews and interviews. Hypothetical example.
SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM
Storytelling

STAR in a team demo or leadership review

"Our onboarding was losing 35% of new users at step 2 (S). We needed to improve activation without adding engineering scope (T). We rewrote two screens, tested two tooltip versions and removed one mandatory field (A). In two weeks activation rose 19% with only copy and configuration changes (R)."

Data

The number that shows the problem and the result.

Emotion

A user quote or moment that makes it real.

Clarity

One message the audience can repeat.

Hypothetical example. Data + emotion + clarity = a story people remember and retell.

SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM
Data

Storytelling with data

  • Title = takeaway: "Checkout loses most users at payment", not "Funnel Q1"
  • Right chart: trend → line, comparison → bar, distribution → histogram
  • Remove clutter; highlight one thing with colour
  • Give context: baseline, target, sample size
  • Show uncertainty: ranges, not false precision
  • End with the action you want
Checkout loses the most users at payment
Cart → Checkout30%
Checkout → Address8%
Address → Payment6%
Payment → Order30%

Stakeholders and decision rights

Map who matters and make it clear who decides.

SkillNavora · Week 6
Stakeholders

Map who matters: the power–interest grid

Keep satisfiedLegal, Finance
Manage closelyVP Product, Head of Payments
MonitorPartner restaurants
Keep informedSupport, Marketing
Interest →Power →
  • High power, high interest: partner closely; bring options, not surprises
  • High power, low interest: short, decision-focused updates
  • Low power, high interest: keep informed; make progress easy to follow
  • Re-map as the project changes; Legal can block a launch late if ignored
Hypothetical placement for a checkout redesign.
SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM
Decision rights

RACI and DACI: who decides?

RACI (for work)

  • Responsible: does the work
  • Accountable: one owner of the outcome
  • Consulted: two-way input
  • Informed: kept updated

DACI (for decisions)

  • Driver runs the process
  • Approver: one person decides
  • Contributors give input
  • Informed hear the result
RoleWho (example)
DriverPM, Checkout
ApproverHead of Product
ContributorsDesign, Eng lead, Analytics, Payments, Legal
InformedSupport, Marketing, Sales
One approver per decision. Writing this down before the debate prevents most escalations. Once decided, disagree and commit: everyone backs the decision, and the dissent is noted.
SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM

Engineering

Negotiating scope with an engineering lead

PM: Our goal is to stop the fee surprise for first-time buyers this quarter. What's the simplest version you'd build?

Eng lead: A static fee is easy. A live estimate needs the pricing service: three weeks, and it's flaky at peak.

PM: What if v1 shows the estimate when the service replies within 500 ms, and 'Estimate unavailable' otherwise?

Eng lead: Then it's about ten days. We'd add a cache later.

PM: Let's take that, behind a flag, as an A/B test. I'll update the PRD and log the cache as a follow-up.

  • Goal first, not a solution
  • Ask for the simplest option
  • Estimates as ranges with assumptions
  • Trade scope, not quality
  • Record the follow-up
  • Story points are team planning tools, not productivity scores
Illustrative dialogue.

08
Part 8

Negotiation and conflict

Find the interests behind the positions.

SkillNavora · Week 6
Negotiation

Positions vs interests

Sales position"Build custom reports for Client X by June."
Product position"Not this quarter, checkout comes first."
Sales interestKeep a ₹40 lakh renewal; the client's finance team needs monthly numbers.
Product interestHit the checkout goal; avoid one-off custom features.
Options that serve bothScheduled CSV export in 2 weeks now · custom reports evaluated in Q3 with evidence from other clients.

From Getting to Yes (Fisher & Ury): separate people from the problem, focus on interests, invent options, use objective criteria, know your BATNA. Example is hypothetical.

SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM
Conflict

Resolving conflict

Five conflict modes (Thomas–Kilmann)

  • Collaborating: important, high-trust issues
  • Compromising: time-bound trade-offs
  • Accommodating: low stakes, build goodwill
  • Competing: urgent, clear-cut calls
  • Avoiding: trivia only

A five-step sequence

  1. Restate each side's interest until they agree you understood
  2. Agree the shared goal and decision criteria
  3. Lay out options with evidence
  4. Decide, or escalate together with a joint summary
  5. Document and move on
SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM

The HiPPO (highest-paid person's opinion)Ask for the goal behind the idea; propose a test; show data respectfully

The silent blocker1:1 conversation; ask what would make them comfortable; involve them early
The scope-creeperPoint to the agreed scope and decision log; queue new asks for the next cycle

Meetings

Anatomy of a decision meeting

Pre-read (T−48h)1-page brief: context, options, recommendation
Frame · 5 minDecision, decider, criteria
Options · 15 minTrade-offs and evidence
Dissent · 10 min"What would make this wrong?"
Decide · 5 minOr name the missing information
Record (T+24h)Decision, rationale, owner, review date
Share an agenda before every meeting and a summary with action items after it. If nobody read the pre-read, read it together for the first five minutes.

Documents

The PRD: a living alignment tool

1 · Summary & decision

Problem, proposal, impact; owner, status

2 · Problem & evidence

Who, what task, why it's hard; data and quotes

3 · Goals & metrics

Primary metric and target; guardrails

4 · Users & use cases

Segments, key scenarios, edge cases

5 · Scope

In and out of scope; assumptions

6 · Requirements

User stories, acceptance criteria, non-functional

7 · Design & analytics

Prototype links; tracking plan

8 · Launch & risks

Rollout, flags, rollback; open questions

Learn from real PRDs: read public PRD templates and examples from companies such as Atlassian, Figma and Lenny's Newsletter, and compare how they handle goals, metrics and scope. Use AI for a first draft, never as the source of truth.
SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM
Documents

User stories and acceptance criteria

User story. As a first-time buyer, I want to see my estimated total in the cart, so that I can decide before I start paying.

INVEST checklist

Independent · Negotiable · Valuable · Estimable · Small · Testable

One-pager before a PRD

Problem, why now, who, approach, impact range, cost, risks, the ask. If it doesn't fit on one page, the idea isn't clear yet.

Acceptance criteria (Given / When / Then)

  • Given an eligible address, when the cart opens, then show item price, estimated fees, taxes and total.
  • Given the fee service fails, when the cart loads, then show "Estimate unavailable" and a Retry button, and never show an invented fee.
  • Given the address changes, when the cart reloads, then refresh the estimate within 2 seconds (p95).
SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM

Feedback and leadership communication

Keep the loop open; deliver bad news well.

SkillNavora · Week 6
Feedback

Feedback is a loop, not an event

SBI: Situation · Behaviour · Impact

"In yesterday's review (S), the PRD's success metric changed from completion to clicks without a note (B). Engineering built tracking for the old metric and lost a day (I). Could we add a change log to the PRD?"

Receiving feedback: thank, clarify, don't defend in the moment, decide what to act on, close the loop.

1 · ContextBe specific
2 · ResponseListen fully
3 · ActionAgree the next step
4 · CloseFollow up

Leadership

Executive reviews and delivering bad news

What executives want

  • The decision you need
  • How it serves the strategy
  • Metrics vs targets, with honest green/amber/red
  • Learnings: what surprised you, what you stopped
  • What you're not doing
  • Anticipate the three hardest questions

Bad news in five sentences

  1. What happened, plainly
  2. The impact
  3. The cause (if known)
  4. What you're doing, and what you need
  5. When you'll update next
"The launch will slip two weeks. A payment-gateway certification took longer than estimated. No customer-facing risk. I recommend waiting rather than launching without the new payment method. I'll update you every Friday."

11
Part 11

AI for PM communication

Faster drafts, better clarity, your judgement.

SkillNavora · Week 6
AI

Use AI to communicate better, not to think less

Good uses

  • Turn messy notes into a structured update
  • Rewrite one message for three audiences
  • Summarise research or long threads
  • Find gaps: "What would an engineer ask?"
  • Draft STAR stories from your notes
  • Check tone before sending difficult messages

Ground rules

  • Never paste confidential or personal data into public tools
  • Check every number, name and claim
  • AI drafts; you decide and own the message
  • Keep your own voice; edit generic phrasing
Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini are all useful here. Use your company's approved tool for work data.

AI prompts

Prompts you can use this week

STAR storyTurn these notes into a STAR story for a PM interview. Keep my actions specific, use only the numbers I give, and flag anything missing: [notes]
Pyramid rewriteRewrite this update using the Pyramid Principle: recommendation first, then 3 reasons with evidence, then the ask. Under 120 words: [update]
Audience versionsWrite three versions of this launch note: for engineers (details), for leadership (impact and risks) and for support (what to tell customers): [note]
Stress testAct as a sceptical CFO. List the 5 hardest questions you'd ask about this proposal and what evidence would convince you: [proposal]
Meeting summarySummarise this meeting transcript into decisions, owners, dates and open questions. Do not invent anything: [transcript]

Part 12

Practice, case study and interview prep

Apply everything from today.

SkillNavora · Week 6
Practice

Exercise: rewrite this update

Original

"We did lots of analysis this week. We looked at funnels, did interviews, talked to payments, and engineering thinks it's 2 months. Fees might be a problem. Also loyalty is pending."

Your turn (5 minutes)

Rewrite it with the Pyramid Principle: answer first, then 2–3 reasons with evidence, then the ask.

Model answer

Recommendation: test showing the delivery fee in the cart from next sprint. Why: (1) 30% of checkout starters leave at payment; (2) 6 of 8 interviewees cite fee surprise; (3) a simplified v1 takes ~2 weeks (full live estimate ~2 months). Ask: approve the two-week v1 and an A/B test; loyalty moves to Q3.
SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM
Case study

Rising cancellations at a home-services app

FixRight (a fictional home-services app for cleaning, plumbing and repairs) has seen booking cancellations rise from 9% to 15% over three months. The CEO wants a recommendation in Friday's leadership review.

In groups (15 minutes)

  1. Who are your stakeholders? Map them on a power–interest grid
  2. Which data would you pull, and from whom?
  3. Write the SCQA opening for Friday's review
  4. Draft the one-page update: findings, options, recommendation, asks

Hints

  • Split cancellations by who cancels: customer or professional
  • Look by category, city, time to job and price shown vs final
  • Talk to support and ops: they hear the reasons first
  • Separate facts, assumptions and next experiments
  • End with a clear ask and the next update date
SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM
This week

Assignment

  1. PRD: FitCircle, a fictional fitness app, wants streaks, rewards and friend challenges to improve 30-day retention. Write a PRD for design and engineering using the template in your LMS.
  2. Executive summary: one screen recommending the launch plan, for the CEO.
  3. Stakeholder map: six stakeholders on a power–interest grid, one action each.
  4. Launch update: the message you'd send on launch day.

Submit in your LMS under Week 6. Written feedback before next week's class.

What good looks like

  • Problem and evidence before features
  • One primary metric plus guardrails (e.g. no rise in injuries or uninstalls)
  • Clear scope: in, out, later
  • Testable acceptance criteria
  • Risks: fairness, cheating, notification fatigue

Interview prep

Communication questions PM interviewers ask

QuestionWhat they're testingAnswer outline
Tell me about a time you influenced without authorityInfluence, evidence, empathySTAR; shared goal, data, options; real result
Describe a conflict with engineering. How did you resolve it?Conflict handling, respectBoth sides' interests; options; decision; relationship after
How would you tell executives a launch is delayed?Bad news, ownership5 sentences; options with a recommendation; next update
How do you handle a stakeholder who keeps adding scope?Prioritisation, boundariesGoal, cost of delay, decision log, next cycle
How do you keep a large cross-functional project aligned?Systems thinkingProject wiki, weekly update, DACI, rituals
Walk me through a PRD you wroteClarity, structureProblem, evidence, metrics, scope, trade-offs, what you'd change
Sales promised a feature to a client. What do you do?Judgement, partnershipUnderstand the interest; options; shared rule for the future
How do you explain a technical trade-off to a non-technical leader?TranslationImpact first, analogy, options, recommendation
SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM
Interview prep

Model answer: "Describe a conflict with engineering"

S: Two weeks before a launch, our tech lead wanted to delay by a sprint to fix performance; sales had already announced the date. T: I needed a decision that protected users without losing the launch. A: I met the tech lead 1:1 to understand the risk, which was slow load times for 20% of Android users. I asked for options: we found we could launch to iOS and high-end Android first and fix performance behind a flag. I wrote a one-page options note and took it to my manager and the sales lead together. R: We launched on time to 80% of users; the rest followed 9 days later with no complaints spike. Learning: bring options, not positions.

Hypothetical model answer: use your own real story and numbers.

Do

  • Say "I" for your actions
  • Show you understood the other side
  • Give the measured result, or say it wasn't measured
  • End with what you learned

Don't

  • Blame the other team
  • Invent numbers
  • Tell a story where you simply escalated
SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM
Interview prep

A 60-second story bank

Prepare five stories before any PM interview. Each one can answer many questions.

  1. A decision you made with incomplete data
  2. A trade-off you negotiated
  3. A stakeholder conflict you resolved
  4. A launch or project that went wrong, and what you learned
  5. A result you are proud of, with numbers

Practise

  • Write each as STAR in under 150 words
  • Say it aloud in 60–90 seconds
  • Prepare follow-ups: "What would you do differently?"
  • Practise with AI as the interviewer, then with a peer
  • Book a mock interview in your LMS
Interviewers often ask for one decision story, one trade-off, one conflict and one measurable result.
SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM
Summary

Key takeaways

Communication is the job

Own the outcome of every message; start from your audience.

Audience · objective · approach

Pick content, channel and cadence on purpose.

Three directions

Core team, upward and outer circle need different things.

Answer first

Pyramid, SCQA and BLUF; MECE reasons with evidence.

Stories that stick

STAR for stories, PREP for quick points, data with a takeaway title.

Decision rights

RACI/DACI, written decisions, disagree and commit.

Interests over positions

Negotiate with options and objective criteria.

Living documents

PRD, wiki, weekly and launch updates keep everyone aligned.

No surprises

Share bad news early with a plan and the next update time.

SkillNavora · Week 6 · Effective Communication as a PM
Cheat sheet

Before you hit send

  • ☐ Who must act, and is it clear in the first line?
  • ☐ Is the answer or ask up front (BLUF)?
  • ☐ Are facts, assumptions and opinions labelled?
  • ☐ Is every number in context?
  • ☐ Is there an owner and a date for each ask?
  • ☐ Is this the right channel?
  • ☐ Would this surprise anyone? Tell them first.
